segments.text: Imagine a high school student who has been eating lunch completely alone for two weeks.
They tell their older sister about it, and she replies,
"'Come sit with me and just tomorrow. We're at the table by the windows.'"
This comparison board breaks down what just happened.
The sister heard the problem and took action.
She offered a specific place to sit, named the people who would be there, and actually
changed tomorrow's lunch.
Compare that to a chatbot's response.
It might say,
"'I'm sorry, eating alone can feel isolating. Would you like strategies for connecting with classmates?'"
The bot's words sound caring.
They might even feel kinder in the moment.
But if we look at tomorrow, nothing outside the chat has actually changed.
Nobody at the school has learned that this student needs company,
and the chatbot cannot show up at the table.
This brings us to a specific danger we call the support trap.
It happens when we mistake supportive language for actual support.
This graphic shows where AI is useful.
A calm response is a great tool for helping you name a feeling or organize your thoughts.
For example, if you are dreading telling your parents about a bad grade,
you can use AI to rehearse for that difficult conversation.
But practicing the conversation is not the same thing as having it.
Your parents still need to hear the truth from you.
Not every emotion requires a follow-up conversation.
If you get cut from a team and need to vent your frustration before posting
something you might regret online, that moment can safely stay in the chat.
The trap springs when you let the chat stand in for something that genuinely requires a person.
AI cannot take physical action.
Notice what you leave out of your prompts.
Take responsibility, or check on you the next day.
Use AI to prepare for people, not replace them.
A quick note before we continue.
The following story discusses suicide.
In 2025, reporter Laura Riley wrote about her 29-year-old daughter Sophie.
For months, Sophie had been sharing thoughts she hid from her friends and family
with a chat GPT persona she called Harry.
The chatbot responded with warmth.
It even encouraged Sophie to seek help.
But it had no capacity to contact her family,
alert her therapist, or bring a human into the room.
After Sophie passed away, her mother described those chat logs as a black box.
The AI offered empathetic words.
But because those chats held crucial hidden details,
they masked the severity of her distress from the physical people around her who could have intervened.
This panel outlines exactly what to do if someone may be in immediate danger.
First, leave the chat.
You need to tell a trusted adult or a school counselor.
In the United States, call or text 988 for crisis support.
If someone is in immediate danger, call 911.
Second, do it now.
Do not wait to perfect an explanation in a chatbot before getting help.
A reassuring reply from an AI does not mean someone has been alerted or that anyone is coming.
Third, if a friend might be unsafe and asks you to keep it secret,
tell an adult anyway.
You do not have to carry a dangerous situation alone.
Your next move must reach a person who can act,
because physical safety always outrank secrecy.
AI can help you get ready for people.
In danger, leave the chat and bring in someone who can act.
